title: Given ropes of different lengths, connecting two ropes costs the sum of their lengths, and the combined rope can be connected again. Find the minimum total cost to connect all ropes into one. Explain why always joining the two shortest ropes is optimal and how a min-heap implements it.
shortTitle: Connect Ropes (Minimum Cost to Connect All Ropes)
keyPoints: Always join the two shortest ropes first because shorter ropes joined early get re-summed in more future merges.
Use a min-heap to always extract the two smallest lengths efficiently.
Each join costs the sum of the two lengths; accumulate that cost and push the combined length back into the heap.
This greedy strategy is provably optimal by the same exchange argument that proves Huffman coding optimal.
Time complexity is O(n log n) for n-1 joins each costing O(log n), and space is O(n) for the heap.
The total cost equals the sum of each original length times its depth in the implicit Huffman tree.

s1_definition.oneliner: Always join the two shortest ropes using a min-heap, accumulate each join's cost, and push the combined rope back until one rope remains.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Greedy choice** – always connect the two shortest ropes first so their lengths participate in the most future sums at the lowest cost.
- **Min-heap** – provides O(log n) extraction of the two smallest lengths and O(log n) insertion of the combined length.
- **Accumulation** – each join's cost (sum of the two lengths) is added to a running total; the final total is the minimum cost.
- **Huffman equivalence** – this is structurally identical to building a Huffman tree, where the total cost equals the sum of each leaf's weight times its depth.
- **Optimality proof** – the exchange argument shows that swapping a shorter rope joined later with a longer rope joined earlier never increases total cost.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the settlement team merges many small daily batches into one final batch. Merging two batches costs effort equal to their combined size, and the merged batch gets merged again later. To minimize total effort, they always merge the two smallest batches first, because their sizes will otherwise be re-counted in every later merge.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Connect Ropes is a greedy optimization problem where the key insight is that ropes joined early participate in more future merges, so their lengths get re-counted more times. By always joining the two shortest ropes first, you ensure the smallest lengths bear the highest re-counting, minimizing total cost. A min-heap makes this efficient by always providing the two smallest lengths in O(log n) time.

The algorithm is straightforward: load all lengths into a min-heap, repeatedly poll the two smallest, add their sum as the join cost to a running total, and push the combined length back. When one rope remains, the total is the minimum cost. This runs in O(n log n) time for n-1 join rounds.

At the National Bank of India, the settlement team used this to merge small daily batches into one final batch, where each merge cost effort proportional to the combined batch size. Always merging the two smallest batches first minimized total effort. The connection to Huffman coding is that the total cost equals the sum of each original length times its depth in the implicit binary tree.

The senior-level insight is the exchange argument for optimality: if you swap a shorter rope joined later with a longer rope joined earlier, the total cost never increases, which formally proves the greedy strategy is optimal.

Remember one sentence: always join the two shortest ropes first with a min-heap, because shorter ropes re-summed more often at lower cost minimizes the total.
